title: Armed with the Mind of Christ
summary: Peter calls suffering believers to break with their old life, serve one another in love, and entrust themselves to God through the fiery trial.
historicalContext: The congregations of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia were made up largely of converts who had once shared fully in the social and religious life of their towns. Trade guild dinners, family festivals, and civic holidays were bound up with sacrifice, heavy drinking, and sexual license, so withdrawal from them was noticed at once and resented as disloyalty to household, city, and gods. The hostility Peter describes is chiefly slander, ostracism, and suspicion, though it could harden into legal accusation and worse. In such communities the name “Christian,” first used by outsiders, could itself become a charge. Peter writes to small, scattered house churches that had no social shelter except one another, preparing them for a deepening ordeal while reminding them that the Judge of the living and the dead sees what their neighbors misjudge and that the Creator they serve keeps faith with his own.
literaryContext: Chapter 4 draws the consequences of 3:18–22. Because Christ suffered in the flesh and now reigns, believers are to take up his resolve and live the rest of their days for God’s will (4:1–6). The nearness of the end then shapes the inner life of the church: clear-minded prayer, persistent love, uncomplaining hospitality, and faithful use of God’s gifts, crowned by a doxology that closes the letter’s long central section (4:7–11). A fresh address, “Beloved,” opens the final movement. Peter returns to the refining fire of 1:6–7, now named a “fiery trial,” and teaches believers to rejoice in sharing Christ’s sufferings, to make sure they suffer only for his name, and to see their testing as the opening of God’s judgment, which begins with his own house (4:12–19). The chapter ends where Christ’s own example ended, with entrusting oneself to the faithful Creator.
themes: Christ’s suffering as the believer’s armor
A decisive break with the former way of life
Universal accountability before the coming Judge
Love, hospitality, and gifts in the household of faith
Judgment beginning at the house of God

outline.title: Done with the Old Life
outline.summary: Armed with Christ’s resolve, believers abandon pagan excess, bear the scorn of former companions, and leave their accusers to the Judge of the living and the dead.

outline.title: Living Near the End
outline.summary: Because the end of all things is at hand, the church gives itself to sober prayer, fervent love, cheerful hospitality, and faithful stewardship of God’s varied grace.

outline.title: Rejoicing in the Fiery Trial
outline.summary: Suffering for Christ is no strange accident; it brings the resting presence of the Spirit and future joy, provided believers suffer for his name and not for wrongdoing.

outline.title: Judgment Begins at God’s House
outline.summary: God’s testing begins with his own people, which sobers believers about the outcome of the disobedient and calls the faithful to entrust themselves to the Creator by doing good.

verses.bibleText: Forasmuch then as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Forasmuch then” gathers up everything Peter has just said about Christ in 3:18–22. The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous, was put to death in the flesh, was made alive by the Spirit, and now sits at God’s right hand with every power made subject to him. Peter does not leave that confession in the realm of doctrine. Its first consequence is a summons: “arm yourselves likewise with the same mind.” The disciple who once drew a sword in Gethsemane now tells the church that its weapon is a settled way of thinking, the resolve Christ carried to the cross.

That resolve was the willingness to obey God whatever obedience cost. Jesus did not stumble into suffering. He set his face toward Jerusalem, prayed “not my will, but thine,” and committed himself to the righteous Judge. Peter’s readers face a smaller but real version of the same choice. They can keep peace with their neighbors by returning to familiar sins, or they can do the will of God and accept the reproach that follows. To arm oneself with Christ’s mind is to settle that question in advance, before the pressure comes.

“He that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin” is best read in that light. Peter is speaking of the believer who has chosen suffering rather than sin. Such a person has shown where his loyalty lies; sin is no longer the master he serves. The words do not claim that a suffering Christian never errs, nor that pain cleanses guilt. Pain can embitter as easily as it refines, and only Christ’s suffering atones. What the phrase describes is a decisive break: the one who would rather bear reproach than return to the old life has turned his back on sin as a way of living.

Peter frames this break through endurance. Each time a believer accepts loss for the sake of obedience, the break with sin is confirmed, and the grace that made the choice possible is shown to be stronger than the old desires.

wordNotes.term: ὁπλίσασθε τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν (hoplisasthe tēn autēn ennoian) — arm yourselves with the same mind
wordNotes.explanation: The verb pictures equipping oneself for combat, as a soldier puts on weapons before battle. The object is ennoia, a way of thinking that issues in conduct: a settled intention or resolve rather than abstract intellect. In the wisdom literature of the Greek Old Testament the word describes the discernment that guards a person’s path. Peter asks believers to take up the same purpose that governed Christ’s obedience unto suffering.

wordNotes.term: πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας (pepautai hamartias) — hath ceased from sin
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect tense describes a settled condition resulting from a past decision. The one who has accepted suffering for obedience stands in a state of having broken with sin. Context rules out a claim of sinless perfection, since Peter goes on to exhort these same believers to love, sobriety, and holiness. The phrase names a changed allegiance: sin no longer directs the life.

verses.bibleText: That he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 2 states the purpose of the armor. The believer is equipped so “that he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.” Two masters stand side by side in the sentence, and the life that remains belongs to one of them. Peter speaks of “the rest of his time,” a phrase that measures life as a limited span. Conversion divides it into a before and an after, and the after is to be wholly redirected.

“In the flesh” here simply means ordinary bodily life on earth, the same sense Peter gave the phrase when speaking of Christ’s death in 3:18. Formerly the “lusts of men,” the desires that ordinary human society approves and feeds, set the direction. Now the will of God does. Peter places the desires in the plural and the will in the singular. Appetites are many, shifting, and competing, while God’s will is one steady purpose.

The words offer both sobriety and hope. They are sober because no one has unlimited time to postpone obedience. They give hope because no past, however long, prevents a person from giving the remaining years to God. The time that remains, spent on God’s will, is the only portion of life that carries forward into eternity.

wordNotes.term: θελήματι θεοῦ (thelēmati theou) — the will of God
wordNotes.explanation: Peter repeatedly names God’s will as the governing reality in the believer’s life. It is God’s will that good conduct silence slander, that believers may suffer for doing right, and that those who suffer entrust themselves to the Creator. The dative here marks the will of God as the standard and aim to which the remaining time of life is devoted.

verses.bibleText: For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now names the life his readers left behind. “The time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles.” There is a touch of irony in the word “suffice.” They have already given that way of life more than enough of their years; it has no further claim. By including himself in “our,” Peter speaks as a fellow sinner rescued by grace, not as a moralist standing above them.

The term “Gentiles” no longer marks ethnicity, since many of the readers were themselves of Gentile birth. Peter has redrawn the line around the people of God, and “the Gentiles” are now those outside that people who live by the desires of the surrounding culture. The six terms that follow describe that culture at its least restrained. “Lasciviousness” is shameless indulgence without restraint; “lusts” are the cravings that drive it; “excess of wine,” “revellings,” and “banquetings” describe the drinking bouts, street processions, and carousing parties that accompanied festivals and guild meetings. Many of these occasions were themselves acts of worship, which is why the list ends with “abominable idolatries,” worship that violates the law of God.

The list carries a quiet lesson about the whole person. Drunkenness, sexual license, and false worship belong together because each surrenders self-control and dulls the mind God gave for knowing him. Scripture’s call to temperance and purity is part of the gospel’s restoration of the human being, body included. Peter will soon urge his readers to be sober for prayer (4:7), and the contrast is deliberate. The clear mind that prays stands opposite the clouded mind of the banquet.

wordNotes.term: τὸ βούλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν (to boulēma tōn ethnōn) — the will of the Gentiles
wordNotes.explanation: Boulēma denotes intention, what someone wishes or plans. Peter deliberately sets the “will of the Gentiles” against the “will of God” in the preceding verse, using a different word but the same contrast. Every life is shaped by someone’s purposes; the question is whose. “Gentiles” here means the unbelieving nations whose desires shape the surrounding culture.

wordNotes.term: ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρίαις (athemitois eidōlolatriais) — abominable idolatries
wordNotes.explanation: Athemitos means unlawful or forbidden, what is contrary to what is right. Applied to idolatry, it marks pagan worship as a breach of the divine order expressed in the first commandments of the Decalogue. The plural suggests the many cults, festivals, and household rites through which idolatry permeated ordinary life.

verses.bibleText: Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The former companions of these believers are bewildered. “They think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot.” The verb describes the surprise a person feels at something foreign and unaccountable. To people who assumed that festivals, drink, and indulgence were simply what life consisted of, the convert’s refusal looked absurd, and perhaps insulting. Family members saw neglect of ancestral rites. Guild members saw disloyalty. Neighbors feared that slighting the gods would bring calamity on the town.

Peter’s image is vivid. The old crowd “runs” together, and what they run into is an “excess of riot,” literally an outpouring or flood of dissipation. The picture is of a torrent sweeping people along, with the Christian standing still while the current rushes past.

Surprise turns to slander: “speaking evil of you.” The Greek verb is the word for blasphemy. Former friends malign the believers, and since the believers are living according to God’s will, the abuse ultimately strikes at God himself. A changed life is a silent rebuke, and people who feel rebuked often respond with ridicule.

Peter does not counsel a return to the old circle for the sake of witness, nor does he tell the believers to retaliate. He simply describes the cost and lets them see it as the expected result of faithfulness. The way forward is to keep living the new life openly and graciously, so that those who now blaspheme may one day glorify God.

wordNotes.term: ξενίζονται (xenizontai) — they think it strange
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is related to xenos, “stranger” or “foreigner,” and means to be surprised by something alien. The word fits a letter addressed to “strangers” (1:1; 2:11): the believers have become foreigners to their old world, and their neighbors find them inexplicable. Peter uses the same verb in 4:12 to tell believers not to treat their trial as strange.

wordNotes.term: τῆς ἀσωτίας ἀνάχυσιν (tēs asōtias anachysin) — the excess of riot
wordNotes.explanation: Anachysis, found only here in the New Testament, means a pouring out or overflow, as of water spreading over the ground. Asōtia describes reckless, wasteful living, the condition of the prodigal son. Together they portray dissipation as a flood that carries people along in its current.

verses.bibleText: Who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The slanderers do not have the last word. “Who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead.” Those who now call the believers to account for their strange behavior will themselves render an account to a higher court.

The Judge is “ready.” Nothing remains to be arranged before he acts; the court is prepared and the verdict awaits only the appointed time. Peter preached the same truth to Cornelius, declaring that God had ordained Jesus to be “the Judge of quick and dead,” and the Father has committed judgment to the Son.

“The quick and the dead” takes in all humanity. Those alive when Christ returns and those who have already died will alike appear before him. Death does not place anyone beyond his reach; the dead are held in God’s keeping until the resurrection, when they will rise to receive the verdict on the life they lived. That universality matters for Peter’s readers. Their persecutors cannot evade God by outliving them or by dying first.

The verse also shapes the believers’ response. Because God will judge, they need not avenge themselves, and they can leave their cause with him as Christ did (2:23). The certainty of judgment, rightly held, produces patience toward opponents rather than bitterness.

wordNotes.term: ἀποδώσουσιν λόγον (apodōsousin logon) — shall give account
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means to render a reckoning, as a steward reports to his master or a debtor settles accounts. Jesus used similar language for the account every person will give for idle words, and Hebrews applies it to those who watch over souls. The future tense makes the reckoning certain.

wordNotes.term: ζῶντας καὶ νεκρούς (zōntas kai nekrous) — the quick and the dead
wordNotes.explanation: “Quick” is older English for “living.” The pairing is a way of saying everyone, those alive at the Lord’s return and those already in the grave. It became part of the church’s early confession of Christ as Judge.

verses.bibleText: For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This verse has often been read as though the dead hear the gospel after death, but its own wording and the context point elsewhere. “For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead.” The phrase “for this cause” ties the verse to verse 5: because a universal judgment is coming, the gospel was preached. The verb is past tense. The preaching had already taken place, and it is not described as continuing. The dead in view are those who are dead now, at the time of writing, and who heard the good news while they were still living.

The word “dead” should carry the same sense in both verses. In verse 5 it means the physically dead who will face judgment, and nothing in verse 6 signals a shift to the spiritually dead. Nor does the verse repeat 3:19, which speaks of Christ proclaiming to “spirits” through Noah’s preaching in Noah’s day. Here the passive verb speaks of the gospel being evangelized to people, with Christ as its content. Scripture teaches that the dead sleep, knowing nothing, until the resurrection, and that the decision of life is made on this side of the grave. The verse offers no second chance after death. Its comfort lies elsewhere.

That comfort answers a real fear. Some believers in Asia Minor had died, perhaps under persecution or simply in the ordinary course of life, and pagans could mock: what good was the gospel, if Christians die like everyone else? Peter replies that the gospel was preached to them during their lifetime precisely so that, though “judged according to men in the flesh,” they might “live according to God in the spirit.” In human estimation their lives looked wasted, their deaths a defeat.

God gives the opposite verdict. Those who received the gospel will live as God lives, raised by the Spirit to immortal life at Christ’s return, just as Christ was “quickened by the Spirit” after being put to death in the flesh (3:18). The contrast between “flesh” and “spirit” follows the pattern of Christ’s own death and resurrection. Death does not cancel the gospel’s promise; it postpones its fulfillment to the morning of the resurrection.

Faithfulness is never lost, even when it ends in a grave. The human court may condemn, but the gospel already heard and believed secures life from God.

wordNotes.term: νεκροῖς εὐηγγελίσθη (nekrois euēngelisthē) — the gospel was preached to them that are dead
wordNotes.explanation: The aorist passive points to a completed act of preaching in the past, not an ongoing proclamation in the realm of the dead. The recipients are “dead” from the standpoint of the time of writing; they heard the good news while they were alive and have since died. The verb, used for announcing good news, differs from the verb for Christ’s proclamation in 3:19, and the recipients differ too: people, not “spirits.”

wordNotes.term: κατὰ ἀνθρώπους … κατὰ θεόν (kata anthrōpous … kata theon) — according to men … according to God
wordNotes.explanation: The two phrases contrast human assessment with divine assessment. In the eyes of people the faithful dead were condemned, their lives judged foolish and their deaths final. In God’s estimation they will live, sharing resurrection life by the Spirit. The structure echoes 3:18, where Christ was put to death in the flesh and quickened by the Spirit.

verses.bibleText: But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the end of all things is at hand.” Peter has just spoken of the Judge who is ready (4:5), and now he widens the view to the close of the whole present order. In the Greek the words “of all things” stand first for emphasis: nothing in creation or history lies outside the conclusion God is bringing. The verb “is at hand” is the one John the Baptist and Jesus used to announce that the kingdom had drawn near. With the death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, history has entered its final stage, and what remains is his appearing in glory.

The New Testament holds this nearness firmly without fixing a date. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour, and Peter will later explain that the Lord’s apparent delay is his patience, not his forgetfulness (2 Peter 3:8–9). “At hand” therefore describes the character of the age more than a countdown. His return will be personal and visible, the revelation of Jesus Christ that Peter has already set before his readers (1:7, 13).

The practical conclusion is striking. Peter does not call for alarm, withdrawal from responsibility, or speculation about timetables. He says, “be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.” The nearness of the end calls for a clear mind and a disciplined life, the opposite of the intoxicated confusion described in verse 3. Its first fruit is prayer. A church that knows the end is near will not be paralyzed by fear or swept along by excitement; it will be found on its knees, alert, steady, and faithful at its post until the Master comes.

wordNotes.term: πάντων δὲ τὸ τέλος ἤγγικεν (pantōn de to telos ēngiken) — the end of all things is at hand
wordNotes.explanation: Telos can mean termination, but also goal or completion, the point toward which a process moves. The perfect tense of engizō, “to draw near,” describes something that has come close and remains close. The same form announces the nearness of the kingdom in the Gospels. Peter speaks of history as having reached its last phase, with the return of Christ as its goal; he gives no date and invites none.

wordNotes.term: σωφρονήσατε … καὶ νήψατε (sōphronēsate … kai nēpsate) — be ye sober, and watch
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb means to be of sound mind, self-controlled, thinking clearly. The second, rendered “watch,” literally means to be sober as opposed to drunk, and by extension alert and vigilant. Together they describe a mind free from intoxication, panic, and distraction, ready for prayer. Peter uses the second verb three times in the letter.

verses.bibleText: And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Of all the duties that follow from the nearness of the end, Peter sets one above the rest: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves.” The love in view is agapē, the self-giving love that seeks another’s good. It is directed “among yourselves,” toward fellow believers. The church Peter addressed was small, scattered, and under pressure from outside. If its members turned on one another, it had nowhere else to go. Jesus had warned that in the last days the love of many would grow cold, and Peter, who heard him say it, insists that love must burn hottest when times are hardest.

“Fervent” translates a word that pictures something stretched out to its full extent, like a runner straining toward the finish or a cord pulled taut. It describes love that persists under strain and keeps reaching toward the other person when feeling might fail.

The reason given is proverbial: “for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.” The saying echoes Proverbs 10:12, where hatred stirs up strife and love covers all offenses. In that setting, covering is the opposite of stirring up. Love does not atone for sin; only Christ’s blood does that (1:18–19). Nor does it pretend wrong has not happened or shelter persistent evil from correction. It declines to broadcast an offense, to rehearse it, or to repay it. When one person absorbs an injury and answers with forgiveness, the chain of retaliation breaks and the wrong dies without multiplying.

In a community where people live closely together, offenses are inevitable. What makes a church endure is less the absence of faults than the presence of love strong enough to cover them. That love is the clearest evidence to a watching world that the gospel has changed its members, and it is the atmosphere in which prayer, hospitality, and service can flourish.

wordNotes.term: ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ (agapēn ektenē) — fervent charity
wordNotes.explanation: Ektenēs comes from a verb meaning to stretch out. It describes intensity sustained over time, earnest and unrelaxed. The cognate adverb describes the church’s earnest prayer for Peter in prison and Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane. The point is constancy more than emotional heat: love that keeps going when it costs something.

wordNotes.term: καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν (kalyptei plēthos hamartiōn) — covers a multitude of sins
wordNotes.explanation: The expression draws on Proverbs 10:12, where love covering offenses is set against hatred stirring up strife. To cover here means to refuse to expose, magnify, or retaliate, so that wrongs within the fellowship are not inflamed. James uses a similar phrase of restoring an erring brother. Neither passage makes human love a means of atonement.

verses.bibleText: Use hospitality one to another without grudging.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Love takes concrete form at the door of a home. “Use hospitality one to another without grudging.” In the first century inns were scarce and often disreputable, and Christian travelers, preachers, and refugees depended on believers to receive them. The churches themselves met in private houses, so a family that opened its home was providing the place where the congregation worshiped, ate together, and prayed.

The Greek word for hospitality combines “love” and “stranger.” For people Peter has called strangers and pilgrims in the world, that is fitting. Those who have no settled home among their neighbors are to make a home for one another.

Peter adds a qualifier that searches motives: “without grudging,” literally without grumbling. Hospitality given with complaint, with sighs about the cost or murmurs about the guests, loses much of its value. Peter asks for an open heart as well as an open door. The cheerful welcome reflects the God who received sinners freely and the Savior who washed his disciples’ feet.

wordNotes.term: φιλόξενοι … ἄνευ γογγυσμοῦ (philoxenoi … aneu gongysmou) — hospitable … without grudging
wordNotes.explanation: Philoxenos means “loving strangers” and is listed among the qualifications of church leaders. Gongysmos, “grumbling,” is an imitative word for low, discontented muttering, the sound Israel made in the wilderness. Peter asks that the welcome be free of resentful complaint, so that the gift and the giver’s spirit agree.

verses.bibleText: As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hospitality is one expression of a wider principle. “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another.” Peter assumes that every believer has received some gift. No member of the church is merely a recipient, and none is excluded from service. The word for gift is closely related to the word for grace. What each person has is a portion of God’s favor, given freely and meant to flow onward to others.

The gifts are to be used “one to another.” Peter is concerned with the life of the congregation. Whatever ability God has given is held in trust for the good of the body.

That trust is expressed in the image of the steward: “as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” A steward in an ancient household managed resources that belonged to his master, distributing provisions to the household and answering for his management. Often he was himself a slave, which made the title striking for believers of low social standing. In the household of God every member holds such an office. The resources are God’s, the beneficiaries are fellow believers, and the steward will give account.

Grace is called “manifold,” the same word Peter used for the “manifold temptations” of 1:6. The variety of God’s grace matches the variety of his people’s trials. For every kind of pressure that bears down on the church, God has distributed among its members a corresponding kind of help. When each one faithfully ministers what has been received, the needs of the whole are met, and no gift proves too small to matter.

wordNotes.term: χάρισμα (charisma) — the gift
wordNotes.explanation: A charisma is a concrete expression of charis, grace. The word covers the full range of God’s endowments, from abilities and opportunities to the specific spiritual gifts listed in Paul’s letters. Peter’s point is that each believer has received something from God’s grace and holds it for the benefit of others.

wordNotes.term: οἰκονόμοι ποικίλης χάριτος θεοῦ (oikonomoi poikilēs charitos theou) — stewards of the manifold grace of God
wordNotes.explanation: An oikonomos was a household manager entrusted with another’s goods for the benefit of the household. Faithfulness was the essential requirement. Poikilos means many-colored or varied. The grace God dispenses through his people is as diverse as the trials they face, and each steward distributes his share.

verses.bibleText: If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter divides the church’s gifts into two broad kinds, speaking and serving, and gives a rule for each. “If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God.” Whoever teaches, exhorts, or counsels in the congregation must do so conscious of handling God’s word. The phrase calls for faithfulness to what God has revealed in Scripture and through the apostolic gospel. The speaker is to bring God’s message to God’s people, not his own speculation or a display of his cleverness, with the seriousness, humility, and clarity that such a task requires.

“If any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth.” Practical service, such as caring for the poor, visiting the sick, preparing meals, or managing the church’s resources, also depends on divine strength. The verb behind “giveth” was used for a benefactor who generously funded a public festival or chorus. God supplies abundantly what his servants need for the work he gives. Service rendered in that strength leaves no room for boasting, because the one serving knows the source of the power.

Both rules serve one purpose: “that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” Words and deeds alike are to point beyond the servant to the God who gives. That glory comes “through Jesus Christ,” the Mediator through whom believers are accepted, empowered, and made able to honor the Father.

The section closes with a doxology: “to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.” The grammar allows the praise to be directed either to God or to Jesus Christ, and Scripture freely gives such honor to both, for the Son shares the Father’s glory. This doxology rounds off the long central portion of the letter. For believers who felt powerless before hostile neighbors, the word “dominion” was a reminder that all power belongs to the God they serve. The “Amen” invites the readers to join their voices to the confession.

wordNotes.term: ὡς λόγια θεοῦ (hōs logia theou) — as the oracles of God
wordNotes.explanation: Logia refers to divine utterances. Stephen used it of the law given at Sinai, and Paul of the Scriptures entrusted to Israel. Peter applies it to the ministry of speaking in the church: those who speak must conform their words to what God has spoken and speak with the reverence that his word deserves.

wordNotes.term: ἐξ ἰσχύος ἧς χορηγεῖ ὁ θεός (ex ischyos hēs chorēgei ho theos) — of the ability which God giveth
wordNotes.explanation: Chorēgeō originally described a wealthy citizen who paid for a dramatic chorus, and came to mean supplying something generously. God is pictured as the lavish provider of strength for every task of service. Paul uses the same verb of God supplying seed to the sower.

verses.bibleText: Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With the tender address “Beloved,” Peter opens the final movement of the letter, as he did at 2:11. He speaks as a pastor who sees a storm gathering over his people and wants them braced for it. “Think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you.” The verb echoes verse 4. The pagans thought it strange that the believers would not join their excess; now the believers must not think it strange that faithfulness brings suffering.

“Fiery trial” recalls the image of 1:7, where faith is tested like gold in the refiner’s fire. The ordeal Peter foresees is severe, yet its purpose is testing, proving what is real. Fire burns away dross; it does not destroy the gold.

Peter’s counsel rests on a realistic view of the conflict between Christ and Satan. As long as that struggle continues over human souls, those who belong to Christ will be targets. The enemy, whom Peter will soon describe as a roaring lion (5:8), aims to destroy faith through pressure and fear. God does not send evil, yet he permits trials, sets their limits, and turns them into occasions for proving and strengthening his children, as the story of Job illustrates.

Why, then, should suffering not seem strange? Because the Master suffered first. Jesus told his disciples that the servant is not greater than his lord, and that a world which hated him would hate them. The fiery trial is the expected path of those who follow a crucified Lord. To know this in advance removes the added pain of bewilderment, the fear that something has gone wrong or that God has forgotten. Nothing foreign is happening. The believers are walking where Christ walked.

wordNotes.term: τῇ ἐν ὑμῖν πυρώσει (tē en hymin pyrōsei) — the fiery trial among you
wordNotes.explanation: Pyrōsis means a burning. In the Greek Old Testament it describes the smelting of metal in a furnace, and in Revelation the burning of Babylon. Peter uses it figuratively for a painful ordeal that tests and purifies faith. The phrase “among you” indicates that it is already present or imminent in the communities.

wordNotes.term: πρὸς πειρασμὸν ὑμῖν (pros peirasmon hymin) — to try you
wordNotes.explanation: Peirasmos can mean temptation to sin or a testing that proves character. Here the latter sense governs: the trial is “for testing,” with a purpose. It is the same word Peter used for the “manifold temptations” of 1:6, where the result is faith proved true.

verses.bibleText: But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Instead of surprise, Peter calls for joy. “But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ’s sufferings.” The ground of rejoicing is fellowship. To suffer for Christ is to share in what he endured, to stand with him in the world’s rejection. The word “partakers” belongs to the vocabulary of fellowship and partnership. Believers do not add anything to Christ’s atoning work; that was finished once for all (3:18). They share in the hostility the world directed at him, which continues against his body, the church.

Peter is not asking believers to enjoy pain. He has already acknowledged that trials bring heaviness (1:6), and he does not ask them to pretend otherwise. The joy rests on what the suffering means and where it leads: “that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.” Present rejoicing looks forward to future rejoicing. The glory of Christ will be revealed at his second coming, openly and before all, and those who shared his reproach will share his triumph.

The Greek doubles the vocabulary of gladness in the final clause, joining the ordinary verb for rejoicing to a stronger word for exultant, leaping joy. It is the same exultation Peter described in 1:6 and 1:8. The rejoicing of the present, real though it is, will be surpassed by the overflowing gladness of that day, when every lonely hour of reproach is swallowed up in the presence of the Lord.

wordNotes.term: κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασιν (koinōneite tois tou Christou pathēmasin) — ye are partakers of Christ’s sufferings
wordNotes.explanation: Koinōneō means to share or have fellowship in something. Believers participate in the suffering that the world inflicted on Christ, as members united to him. Paul expresses the same idea as knowing “the fellowship of his sufferings.” Such participation is the pathway to sharing his glory.

wordNotes.term: χαρῆτε ἀγαλλιώμενοι (charēte agalliōmenoi) — ye may be glad also with exceeding joy
wordNotes.explanation: Peter joins chairō, “to rejoice,” with agalliaō, “to exult” or “leap for joy.” The second verb often marks the overflowing gladness of God’s people at his saving acts. The combination describes the full, unrestrained joy that will attend Christ’s appearing.

verses.bibleText: If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now applies the Lord’s own beatitude to his readers. “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye.” Jesus had said, “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you … for my sake.” The verb for reproach describes insult, ridicule, and verbal abuse, the kind of slander that often prepares the way for harsher persecution. Such reproach is “for the name of Christ,” on account of belonging to him and bearing his name.

The reason follows: “for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you.” The words echo Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the Lord rests on the coming shoot from Jesse’s stem. What was promised to the Messiah now rests on those who suffer for his sake. The Holy Spirit is called “the spirit of glory,” because he is the pledge and foretaste of the glory to be revealed (v. 13). Those who suffer reproach for Christ already carry something of that coming glory.

The verb “resteth” suggests abiding presence and refreshment, the Spirit settling on a person and remaining. Every believer has the Spirit, yet Scripture shows that God draws especially near to those who suffer for him. Stephen, facing a hostile council, was full of the Holy Ghost and saw the glory of God. Jesus promised that the Spirit would give his disciples words when they were brought before rulers. The believer under reproach is never abandoned. The very hour of insult is an hour of divine presence.

The final clause, “on his part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified,” is absent from many of the oldest manuscripts, though its thought fits the context well. When opponents revile believers for Christ’s sake, they are really reviling the Spirit who rests on them; when believers endure faithfully, they bring glory to God.

wordNotes.term: ὀνειδίζεσθε ἐν ὀνόματι Χριστοῦ (oneidizesthe en onomati Christou) — ye be reproached for the name of Christ
wordNotes.explanation: Oneidizō means to heap insults upon, to revile or disgrace. It is the verb Jesus used in the beatitude on the persecuted, and Hebrews speaks of bearing Christ’s reproach. “For the name of Christ” means because of identification with him, because believers bear his name and confess him as Lord.

wordNotes.term: τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα … ἀναπαύεται (to tēs doxēs kai to tou theou pneuma … anapauetai) — the spirit of glory and of God resteth
wordNotes.explanation: The Holy Spirit is identified as the Spirit who belongs to glory and to God. The verb anapauō, used in the Greek of Isaiah 11:2 for the Spirit resting on the Messiah, means to come to rest upon, to settle, and also to refresh. The Spirit who rested on Christ rests on those who suffer for him.

verses.bibleText: But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The blessing of verse 14 belongs only to those who suffer for the right reason, so Peter adds a sober qualification. “But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men’s matters.” Throughout the letter he has insisted that there is no credit in suffering deserved punishment (2:20; 3:17).

The list moves from grave crimes to a lesser fault. Murder and theft were forbidden by the commandments and punished by Roman law. “Evildoer” is a broad term for any criminal or wrongdoer. Peter does not suggest that his readers were committing such crimes; Christians were sometimes falsely accused of them, and he wants every accusation to be plainly false.

The last item is unexpected. “Busybody in other men’s matters” translates a rare compound word, perhaps coined for the occasion, that pictures someone acting as overseer of other people’s affairs. Peter may be thinking of believers who, in zeal for their new faith, criticized pagan customs tactlessly, interfered in family matters, or pressed their convictions on others in ways that provoked needless hostility. If they must suffer, let it be for Christ, and for nothing they could have avoided by humility and discretion.

wordNotes.term: ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος (allotriepiskopos) — busybody in other men’s matters
wordNotes.explanation: This compound joins allotrios, “belonging to another,” with episkopos, “overseer.” It appears nowhere earlier in Greek literature, so its exact sense must be drawn from its parts and context. It suggests one who takes it upon himself to supervise matters that are not his responsibility, a meddler or self-appointed judge of others. Paul warns against similar behavior using different words.

verses.bibleText: Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having excluded suffering for wrongdoing, Peter turns to the suffering that brings honor. “Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.” The name “Christian” appears only three times in the New Testament. Believers were first called by it at Antioch, apparently by outsiders, and King Agrippa used it in conversation with Paul. Here it describes a charge: a person might suffer simply for being known as one who belongs to Christ.

In the social world of the first century honor and shame carried enormous weight. To be publicly shamed was a grievous loss, and opponents used ridicule to push believers back into conformity. Peter refuses that verdict. “Let him not be ashamed.” The believer is not to accept the world’s reckoning of what is honorable. To be identified with Christ is the highest honor a person can bear, whatever the surrounding society thinks. Peter himself had once been ashamed of Jesus in a high priest’s courtyard. Now, restored by grace and having faced councils and prisons, he urges others never to be ashamed of the name.

The positive command is “let him glorify God on this behalf.” Many manuscripts read “in this name,” which fits the sense well. The believer praises God for the privilege of bearing Christ’s name and sharing his reproach. The apostles after their beating in Jerusalem departed “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name.” The name that the world uses as an accusation becomes, in the believer’s mouth, a reason for thanksgiving.

wordNotes.term: ὡς Χριστιανός (hōs Christianos) — as a Christian
wordNotes.explanation: The suffix -ianos was used for partisans or adherents of a person, as Herodians were followers of Herod. “Christian” thus meant “one of Christ’s people.” Its three New Testament occurrences all reflect usage by outsiders, and Roman sources show that by the early second century the name alone could bring believers before a magistrate.

wordNotes.term: μὴ αἰσχυνέσθω (mē aischynesthō) — let him not be ashamed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to feel or be put to shame. In Scripture shame is overcome by confident trust in God, who vindicates those who believe. Paul declares that he is not ashamed of the gospel, and Jesus warned against being ashamed of him and his words.

verses.bibleText: For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now places the believers’ suffering within the larger work of God’s judgment. “For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God.” The word “time” here denotes an appointed season, the moment fixed in God’s plan. With the coming of Christ the last days have begun, and the judgment that will finally encompass all humanity has started with those who profess God’s name.

“The house of God” is the church, the spiritual house built of living stones that Peter described in 2:5. The idea that judgment starts at God’s house runs through the prophets. In Ezekiel’s vision the executioners were told, “begin at my sanctuary,” and they started with the elders standing before the temple, though first a mark was set on those who sighed over the abominations done in the city. Malachi foretold that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple and sit as a refiner, purifying the sons of Levi. The consistent pattern is that God deals first with those who bear his name and then with the world.

Peter adapts that pattern with a significant change. In the prophets, judgment began at the sanctuary because of the people’s sin. Here the believers suffer because of their faithfulness. The fiery trial (v. 12) is God’s testing of his household, a sifting that shows who truly belongs to Christ. The word for judgment can describe the act of judging, the evaluation itself, without implying condemnation. Through persecution God brings to light what is real and separates it from mere profession, in keeping with the scriptural picture of a judgment in which the lives of God’s professed people are reviewed before the final reckoning of the world.

The second half of the verse draws an inference that should sober every reader: “and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?” If God’s own people must pass through the refining fire, what awaits those who reject his message entirely? He offers no pleasure in the fate of the disobedient, only a solemn question that urges perseverance among believers and leaves the door of repentance open to all who still have time to obey.

wordNotes.term: ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ ἄρξασθαι τὸ κρίμα (ho kairos tou arxasthai to krima) — the time is come that judgment must begin
wordNotes.explanation: Kairos denotes a fitting or appointed time, a moment of opportunity within God’s purposes, as in the “time” of Christ’s coming that the prophets searched for. Krima can mean either a sentence of condemnation or the process of judging. Since Peter is speaking of the testing of faithful believers, the latter sense fits: God has begun his work of evaluation with his own people.

wordNotes.term: ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ θεοῦ (apo tou oikou tou theou) — at the house of God
wordNotes.explanation: In the Old Testament “the house of God” is the temple; in the New Testament it is the community of believers, God’s dwelling by the Spirit. Peter has already called the church a spiritual house. The phrase links the church’s present trial with the prophetic pattern of judgment beginning at the sanctuary.

verses.bibleText: And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter reinforces the question of verse 17 with Scripture, citing Proverbs 11:31 in its Greek form: “And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” The argument moves from the lesser to the greater. If even those who belong to God reach salvation only through severe testing, how will those who have refused him stand on the day of judgment?

“Scarcely” means with difficulty. The point is not that God’s power to save is in doubt or that salvation hangs by a thread of human effort. The righteous are saved by grace through the merits of Christ alone, and they are kept by the power of God through faith (1:5). Yet the path to final salvation runs through trials, temptations, and pressures that test faith to the uttermost. Many who begin the journey turn back under pressure. Those who arrive do so because God holds them fast, and they arrive having passed through fire.

The question “where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” is left unanswered, and the silence speaks. The psalmist declared that the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, and that their way shall perish. Scripture describes the end of those who finally reject God’s mercy as destruction, the loss of the life they refused to receive from him. That is no endless existence in torment; it is the final ruin of a life cut off from its Source. Peter raises the question to warn rather than to gloat. It reminds believers that present suffering, however painful, is small compared with the loss awaiting those who reject the gospel, and it calls them to persevere in the grace that carries the righteous through.

wordNotes.term: μόλις σῴζεται (molis sōzetai) — scarcely be saved
wordNotes.explanation: Molis means with difficulty, hardly, barely. Luke uses it of a ship struggling against contrary winds. Here it describes the arduous path through which the righteous reach salvation, not uncertainty about God’s ability to save. The phrase comes from the Greek rendering of Proverbs 11:31.

wordNotes.term: ποῦ φανεῖται (pou phaneitai) — where shall … appear
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to appear or be seen. The rhetorical question implies that the ungodly will find no place to stand before the Judge. Scripture speaks of the wicked unable to stand in the judgment and of the place of the wicked being sought and not found.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter gathers the whole section into a final exhortation. “Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.” “According to the will of God” excludes suffering brought on by wrongdoing (v. 15). It describes suffering that comes because the believer is doing what God wills, and that happens within God’s permission and purpose. Such suffering is never outside his knowledge or control.

The verb “commit” means to deposit something with another for safekeeping, as one entrusts valuables to a reliable guardian. It is the very word Jesus used on the cross: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” Peter has already shown Christ committing himself to the One who judges righteously (2:23). Believers are to do the same, placing their “souls,” their lives, their whole selves, in God’s care. The word here points to the person as a living being; it carries no idea of a part that survives death on its own. Life itself is what is entrusted to God, and he will keep it through suffering, death, and the grave until he restores it at the resurrection.

This entrusting happens “in well doing.” Trust in God does not lead to passivity or retreat. Believers keep doing good, the very conduct that may provoke hostility. They continue in honest work, respectful conduct, gentle answers, and loving service, leaving the outcome with God.

God is called “a faithful Creator,” a title found only here in the New Testament. As Creator he made all things and governs all things, including the persecutors and the trial itself. As faithful he keeps his promises and never abandons those who trust him. The one who formed human life is able to preserve it and to raise it again. For believers facing a hostile world, there is no safer place to deposit their lives than in the hands of the God who made them and has pledged himself to them.

wordNotes.term: παρατιθέσθωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν (paratithesthōsan tas psychas autōn) — commit the keeping of their souls
wordNotes.explanation: Paratithēmi means to place beside, to deposit in trust. It is the verb of Psalm 31:5 in Greek and of Jesus’ dying words. Psychē here means life or self, the whole person. Believers entrust their very lives to God for safekeeping until he restores them.

wordNotes.term: πιστῷ κτίστῃ (pistō ktistē) — a faithful Creator
wordNotes.explanation: Ktistēs, “Creator,” occurs only here in the New Testament. It grounds trust in God’s power as the maker and ruler of all things. Pistos, “faithful,” stresses his reliability: he keeps faith with what he has made and with his covenant people. Creation and faithfulness together assure the sufferer that his life is in capable and dependable hands.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would change in a believer’s choices if he expected faithfulness to cost him something rather than spare him every trouble?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Because Christ suffered and now reigns, believers arm themselves with his resolve, live for God’s will in a loving community, and entrust themselves to the faithful Creator when obedience brings suffering.
discussionQuestions: In what sense has the one who suffers in the flesh “ceased from sin,” and what does Peter not claim by that phrase?
Why does Peter place prayer, love, hospitality, and service immediately after announcing that the end is at hand?
How can suffering for Christ be a cause for joy without making pain itself desirable?
What distinguishes suffering “as a Christian” from trouble brought on by meddling or misconduct?
Why would God’s judgment begin with his own house, and how does that comfort rather than terrify the faithful?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 6 does not teach that the dead hear the gospel after death; it speaks of those who heard it while living and have since died.
Love that “covers a multitude of sins” does not hide wrongdoing or atone for it; it refuses to keep offenses alive and spreading.
Not all hardship is suffering for Christ; Peter separates suffering for his name from consequences of one’s own wrong.
The nearness of the end calls for sober duty and prayer, never for date-setting or abandonment of daily responsibilities.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the believer’s decisive break with sin and the community’s mutual care: the same grace that arms the individual with Christ’s mind equips the church to love, serve, and endure together.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Take up the mind of Christ, spend the time that remains for the will of God, and when obedience costs you, commit yourself into the hands of the faithful Creator.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ suffered for sinners and will judge the living and the dead; those who receive the gospel in this life break with sin and await resurrection life from God.
flow: Every person will give account to the One ready to judge the living and the dead.
Christ suffered in the flesh for us, bearing sin so that we might be brought to God.
The gospel is preached now, in this life, so that people may turn while there is time.
Those who receive it leave the old way and live the rest of their time for God’s will.
Whatever the world’s verdict, God raises his own to life at Christ’s appearing.
simpleIllustrations: A soldier who has truly enlisted no longer takes orders from the camp he left, even when his old friends call him back.
A refiner’s fire does not destroy the gold; it removes what does not belong and shows the metal for what it is.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let the time already spent on your own way be enough, and give the rest of your life to the will of God?
cautions: Do not present suffering as a means of earning forgiveness; Christ’s suffering alone deals with sin.
Do not use verse 6 to offer hope of a second chance after death.
Do not portray former companions as enemies to be despised; Peter leaves judgment with God and keeps the door of witness open.

reflectionQuestions: What part of my former way of life still tugs at me, and have I let the time already spent on it be enough?
When others misunderstand my faith, do I answer with resentment or with the confidence that God will judge rightly?
Which gift of God’s varied grace have I received, and whom am I serving with it this week?
Is my hospitality given freely, or does it carry a hidden murmur of complaint?
When obedience costs me, how am I entrusting myself to the faithful Creator while continuing to do good?
